We consider a nonlinear, strongly coupled, parabolic system arising in the modeling of burglary in residential areas. The system is of chemotaxis-type and involves a logarithmic sensivity function and specific interaction and relaxation terms. Under suitable assumptions on the data of the problem, we give a rigorous proof of the existence of a global and bounded, classical solution, thereby solving a problem left open in previous work on this model. Our proofs are based on the construction of approximate entropies and on the use of various functional inequalities. We also provide explicit numerical conditions for global existence when the domain in a square, including concrete cases involving values of the parameters which are expected to be physically relevant.

1. Introduction

1.1. Model and main results

In a series of recent papers, models based on partial differential equations have been derived to study crime, see [3], [8, 18, 19, 21, 22]. Some of these papers are most related to modeling burglary of houses. A basic issue here is to obtain patterns that describe the location of hotspots, and study phenomena such as appearance and disappearance of them, their stability and movement.

A very successful model was obtained recently by Short et al. in [22]. They first derived an agent-based statistical model to study the dynamics of hotspots, taking two sociological effects into account: the ‘broken window effect’ and the ‘repeat near-repeat effect’. The first effect refers to the observation that crime in an area leads to more crime, and the second one to the observation that houses burglarized at some moment have an increased probability of being burglarized again for some period of time after that moment.

The agent-based model considered relies on the assumption that criminal agents are walking randomly on a two-dimensional lattice and are committing burglaries when encountering an attractive opportunity. An attractiveness value is assigned to every house, which measures how easily the house can be burgled without consequences for the criminal agent. In addition to be walking randomly, the criminal agents move toward areas of high attractiveness values. In turn, when a burglary occurs, it increases the attractiveness of the house that was burglarized and of those nearby. If no additional burglaries occur, then the local attractiveness decays toward a constant value.

In a second step, by taking a suitable limit of the equations for the discrete model, the authors in [22] obtained the following system of parabolic differential equations (in adimensionalized form):

{∂A∂t=η​△​A+N​A+A0−A,∂N∂t=∇⋅[∇N−N∇ϑ(A)]−NA+A¯−A0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}=\eta\triangle A+NA+A^{0}-A,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial N}{\partial t}=\nabla\cdot\Bigr[\nabla N-N\nabla\vartheta(A)\Bigl]-NA+\overline{A}-A^{0}.\end{array}\right. (1)

Here and thoughout this article, we denote

ϑ⁡(A)=χ​log⁡A,with χ>0 constant.\vartheta(A)=\chi\log A,\quad\hbox{with $\chi>0$ constant.} (2)

The model described in [22] involves the specific value χ=2\chi=2 (we note that the parameter χ\chi cannot be scaled out by a linear change of dependent or independent variables). The functions A⁡(x,t)A(x;t) and N⁡(x,t)N(x,t) respectively represent the attractiveness value and the criminal density at position xx and time tt. The first equation describes the evolution of the attractiveness of individual houses to burglary, and the second describes the burglar movement. Here Ω\Omega is a bounded domain in ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, η>0\eta>0 is the diffusion rate of attractiveness, A0A^{0} is the intrinsic attractiveness, A¯\overline{A} is a contant that in the equilibrium case represents the average attractiveness.

A first effort to study the dynamics of the model represented by problem (1) was done in [19], where a corresponding initial-boundary value problem with no flux boundary conditions is considered. To deal with this problem, the authors in [19] assume, for simplicity, that Ω\Omega is a square and under some symmetry conditions are able to map this problem into one with periodic problem boundary conditions. Their main result is local existence of a solution, but global existence is left open. In addition, and as a simplification of the model in [22], they considered a generalized version of a Keller-Segel chemotaxis model with the goal of understanding possible conditions for global existence vs blow-up of solutions in finite time for the original model.

In [22], an important hypothesis is that burglars are generated in the model at a constant rate and leave the lattice immediately after they have committed a burglary. In [18], a modified agent-based model for burglary was obtained, a new condition is introduced to modify these effects. This new condition, that is refer as burglar fatigue, models the effect that if burglars are sufficiently deterred, they will eventually get tired and will stop looking for houses to burglar. This consideration introduces changes to the original equations of Short et al. Some additional changes to the original equations come in by considering in the model that, if too many burglaries occur at some location, then burglars are likely to assume that most of the high-value is gone or that the owners of the place have implemented more strict security measures.

As in the original model, by taking the continuous limit to this new agent-based model, a new system of parabolic equations is obtained in [18]. This system, complemented with initial data and no-flux boundary conditions, leads us to study the following initial-boundary value problem (again in adimensionalized form):

{∂A∂t=η​Δ​A+ψ​N​A​(1−A)+A~−A,x∈Ω,t>0,∂N∂t=∇⋅[∇N−N∇ϑ(A)]+ω−ωN,x∈Ω,t>0,∂A∂ν=∂N∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,A(x,0)=A0(x),N(x,0)=N0(x),x∈Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}=\eta\Delta A+\psi NA(1-A)+\tilde{A}-A,&\quad x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial N}{\partial t}=\nabla\cdot\Bigr[\nabla N-N\nabla\vartheta(A)\Bigl]+\omega-\omega N,&\quad x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial A}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial\nu}=0,&\quad x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \\ A(x,0)=A_{0}(x),\quad N(x,0)=N_{0}(x),&\quad x\in\Omega.\end{array}\right. (3)

Here again the function ϑ\vartheta is defined by (2) with χ=2\chi=2 in [18]. Moreover, it is assumed – as we will do throughout this paper – that

Ω\Omega is a sufficiently smooth bounded domain of ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2}, or a square, (4)
η,ψ,ω,A~>0\eta,\psi,\omega,\tilde{A}>0 are constants (5)

and that the initial data satisfy

(A0,N0)∈H1+β​(Ω)×L2​(Ω)(A_{0},N_{0})\in H^{1+\beta}(\Omega)\times L^{2}(\Omega) for some β>0\beta>0, with A0>0A_{0}>0 in Ω¯\overline{\Omega} and N0≥0N_{0}\geq 0 a.e. in Ω\Omega. (6)

The outward normal vector on ∂Ω\partial\Omega is denoted by ν\nu. (We point out that all the functional analytic properties needed for the proofs remain true in a square, although the latter is not smooth at the corner points.) Problem (3) is locally well posed, the positivity of AA being of course understood as part of the definition of solution (see Section 2 for details).

In [18], some results about linearized stability/instability of the homogeneous steady-states and some numerical simulations suggesting the existence of hotspots were given for system (3). However, the (local and) global existence of solutions was left open.

In this paper, our main goal is to give a rigorous proof of the global existence and boundedness of solutions of system (3) under suitable assumptions. In what follows, we denote

ε0=ε0(Ω)=μ−2K−1/2,\varepsilon_{0}=\varepsilon_{0}(\Omega)=\mu^{-2}K^{-1/2},

Assume (2), (4)-(6) and

(AmaxAmin)2​(Amax−Amin)​max⁡{‖N0‖1,|Ω|}<ε0​η​ψ−1​χ−2.\Bigl(\frac{A_{\max}}{A_{\min}}\Bigr)^{2}(A_{\max}-A_{\min})\max\{\|N_{0}\|_{1},|\Omega|\}<\varepsilon_{0}{\hskip 1.0pt}\eta{\hskip 1.0pt}\psi^{-1}\chi^{-2}. (7)

1.2. Explicit global existence conditions and discussion

Interestingly, in view of practical applications, the constant appearing in Theorem 1.1 can be estimated explicitly in the case of a square.

Theorem 1.3.

Let Ω=(0,L)2\Omega=(0,L)^{2}, with L>0L>0. Then the result of Theorem 1.1 is true with

ε0=13​3≈0.19.\varepsilon_{0}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\approx 0.19.

With Theorem 1.3 at hand, we shall now explicitly compute our sufficient condition for global existence and boundedness in concrete cases involving values of the parameters which are expected to be physically relevant (cf. [22, 18]). The parameters of system (3) are expressed in [18] in terms of parameters of the dimensional form of the model. To avoid confusion, dimensional parameters are marked with a hat in what follows.

The domain is taken to be a square lattice where exactly one house is located at each lattice site. Distances are thus measured in units of house separations and the adimensional side length of the domain is thus essentially equal to p\sqrt{p}, where p≫1p\gg 1 is the total number of houses. After a suitable renormalization (involving the diffusion and mean lifetime parameters of the burglars – see table 1 and formula (3.3) in [18, p.406]), the measure of the adimensionalized spatial domain Ω\Omega is given by |Ω|=p/3500|\Omega|=p/3500. We chose p=3500p=3500, hence |Ω|=1|\Omega|=1. Next, the parameter ω\omega is given by ω=ω^2/ω^1\omega=\hat{\omega}_{2}/\hat{\omega}_{1}, where ω^1\hat{\omega}_{1} and ω^2\hat{\omega}_{2} are the mean lifetimes of the attractiveness and of the active burglars, respectively. The values chosen in [18] are ω^1=(1/14)​day−1\hat{\omega}_{1}=(1/14)\,{\rm day}^{-1} and ω^2=6​day−1\hat{\omega}_{2}=6\,{\rm day}^{-1}, hence ω=84\omega=84. The parameter ψ\psi is given by ψ=θ^​Γ^/ω^1​ω^2\psi=\hat{\theta}\hat{\Gamma}/\hat{\omega}_{1}\hat{\omega}_{2}, where Γ^\hat{\Gamma}, describing the source term, stands for the number of burglars becoming active per time and surface unit and θ^\hat{\theta} is the factor that boosts attractiveness due to a burglary. We take Γ^=0.002​burglars⋅day−1⋅house​separation−2\hat{\Gamma}=0.002\ {\rm burglars}\cdot{\rm day}^{-1}\cdot{\rm house\ separation}^{-2}, which is the value taken in [22] for the analogous parameter (the value Γ^=0.5\hat{\Gamma}=0.5 used in [18] seems too high, apparently due to a lack of spatial normalization). For the domain that we consider, this means a total source term of 7​burglars⋅day−17\ {\rm burglars}\cdot{\rm day}^{-1}. Concerning θ^\hat{\theta}, following [18], we take θ^=1​burglars−1⋅day−1\hat{\theta}=1\ {\rm burglars}^{-1}\cdot{\rm day}^{-1}, which leads to ψ=(14/3)×10−3≈0.0047\psi=(14/3)\times 10^{-3}\approx 0.0047. As for the attractiveness diffusion parameter η\eta, which models neighboring effects, smaller values mean that repeat victimization is more and more likely than near-repeat victimization. The values taken in [22] range from 0.010.01 to 0.20.2, whereas [18] takes η=0.001\eta=0.001.

Last, let us consider the initial data. Concerning the (adimensional) attractiveness AA, recall that the constant A~\tilde{A} is assumed to represent its static component, while A−A~A-\tilde{A} represents the dynamic component associated with the boost hypothesis. A~≤A0​(x)≤1,\tilde{A}\leq A_{0}(x)\leq 1, (10)

A~−2​(1−A~)<γ​η, where ​γ=112​3​(|Ω|​ψ)−1=125​321≈10.31.\tilde{A}^{-2}(1-\tilde{A})<\gamma\,\eta,\quad\hbox{ where }\gamma=\frac{1}{12\sqrt{3}}{\hskip 1.0pt}(|\Omega|\psi)^{-1}=\frac{125\sqrt{3}}{21}\approx 10.31. (11)

1.3. Related results and comments

As noted in [22], problems (1) and (3) belong to the family of chemotaxis-type systems. A more general class of such systems takes the form

{∂A∂t=η​Δ​A−A+f⁡(A,N),∂N∂t=ΔN−∇(N∇h(A))−ωN+g(A,N).\displaystyle\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}=\eta\Delta A-A+f(A,N),\\ \\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial N}{\partial t}=\Delta N-\nabla(N\nabla h(A))-\omega N+g(A,N).\end{cases} (12)

The typical feature of chemotaxis-type systems is the presence of the antidiffusion term, here −∇(N∇h(A))-\nabla(N\nabla h(A)), by which the population, of density NN, tends to move towards higher concentrations of AA. The best-known among this class of problems is the Keller-Segel model [14], corresponding to f=Nf=N, h=Ah=A and g=0g=0. There is a very large literature on such systems (see [11, 12], for recent surveys).

System (12) with a logarithmic sensivity function h=χ​log⁡(A)h=\chi\log(A) was considered in [4, 23] for f=Nf=N and g=ω=0g=\omega=0. Without any size restriction on the initial data, existence of a global classical solution was proved in [4] under the restriction χ≤1\chi\leq 1, whereas existence of a (possibly singular) global weak solution was proved in  [23] for any χ>0\chi>0. System (12) with a logarithmic sensivity function was also considered in [2] (see also [17]), in conjunction with a quadratic absorption term, namely g=−c​N2g=-cN^{2}, and f=Nf=N. In this case, global classical existence was proved for any χ>0\chi>0 without size restriction on the initial data, but the proof made crucial use of the quadratic absorption term.

Here, with only a linear absorption −ω​N-\omega N and the specific ff under consideration, a size condition on the initial data is required to prove existence of global classical solution, but we do not need absolute restrictions on the parameter χ\chi. Although we do not know what happens for larger initial data, let us recall that in the case of the Keller-Segel model in two space dimensions, global existence is true only for small initial mass and that blow-up may occur for large mass. However proving blow-up for 22-dimensional parabolic chemotaxis models is a very challenging task. The only known blow-up result for the 2​d2d Keller-Segel system is that of Herrero and Velázquez [10], and its proof, based on matched asymptotics, is highly technical. In simplified parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis models, where the term ∂A/∂t\partial A/\partial t in (12) is replaced by 00, blow-up proofs are easier and there are more results available. In particular, when h=χ​log⁡Ah=\chi\log A, f=Nf=N, g=ω=0g=\omega=0 and the space dimension nn is at least 33, finite time blow-up is known [15] to occur for χ>2​n/(n−2)\chi>2n/(n-2). For blow-up results concerning the parabolic-elliptic Keller-Segel system, see e.g. the survey [6].

Our global existence proofs, as is customary in chemotaxis-type problems, rely on a priori estimates obtained by energy and entropy arguments. However, in the case of Theorem 1.1, some care is needed to properly take into account the size condition on the initial data. In the case of the Keller-Segel system, an exact entropy functional was found and used to prove global existence for suitably small mass in [16, 9, 4]. Although system (3) is not known to possess an exact entropy functional, assuming condition (7) on the data of the problem, we can nevertheless construct an approximate entropy functional (with the typical N​log⁡NN\log N growth – cf. Lemma 3.1), which is the key to our a priori estimates. We also stress that, in spite of uniform lower and upper bounds for AA which easily follow from the maximum principle, the proof of the estimates of NN is far from being immediate. As for Theorem 1.2, under the assumptions χ≤1\chi\leq 1, A~≤1\tilde{A}\leq 1 and maxΩ¯⁡A0≤1\displaystyle\max_{\overline{\Omega}}A_{0}\leq 1, we can use a modified entropy functional from [5].

    |f⁡(A,N)|≤f1​(A)​N+f2​(A),|f(A,N)|\leq f_{1}(A)N+f_{2}(A),

The outline of the rest of the article is as follows. Subsection 2.1 is devoted to local existence and uniqueness, whereas Subsection 2.2 contrains basic estimates, energy identities and functional inequalities which will needed for proving global existence. Sections 3–5 are then devoted to the proofs of Theorems 1.1, 1.3 and 1.2, respectively. Finally, our main conclusions are summarized in Section 6.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Local existence and uniqueness

We have the following local existence and uniqueness result.

Proposition 2.1.

Assume (2), (4)-(6) and fix any β∈(0,12)\beta\in(0,\frac{1}{2}). Then problem (3) admits a unique, classical, maximal in time solution (A,N)(A,N) with A>0A>0. Moreover, if its maximal existence time T∗T^{*} is finite, then limt→T∗‖A⁡(t)‖H1+β+‖N⁡(t)‖L2=∞\lim_{t\to T^{*}}\|A(t)\|_{H^{1+\beta}}+\|N(t)\|_{L^{2}}=\infty.

Note that the solution given by Proposition 2.1 is of course independent of the choice of β∈(0,12)\beta\in(0,\frac{1}{2}) (due to local uniqueness and the fact that H1+β​(Ω)⊂H1+γ​(Ω)H^{1+\beta}(\Omega)\subset H^{1+\gamma}(\Omega) for β>γ\beta>\gamma). The procedure for proving Proposition 2.1 is rather standard (see, e.g., [17, 2, 13] for more details on similar problems). Although the function ϑ\vartheta is singular at A=0A=0, this actually causes no difficulty, because a positive lower bound for AA can be deduced from the maximum principle (first working with a smooth replacement of ϑ\vartheta). We sketch the proof for completeness.

We first recall some properties of theory of abstract evolution equation. Let ℋ,𝒱\mathcal{H},\mathcal{V} be two separable Hilbert spaces with dense and compact embedding 𝒱⊂ℋ\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{H}. Identifying ℋ\mathcal{H} with its dual ℋ′\mathcal{H}^{\prime} and denoting the dual space of 𝒱\mathcal{V} by 𝒱′\mathcal{V}^{\prime}.

Consider the initial value problem

Then

The linear operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} is defined by

where T1=−Δ+1T_{1}=-\Delta+1 is regarded as an operator from HN2+β​(Ω)H^{2+\beta}_{N}(\Omega) to Hβ​(Ω)H^{\beta}(\Omega) and T2=−Δ+ωT_{2}=-\Delta+\omega is the Laplace operator equipped with the Neumann boundary condition in H1​(Ω)′H^{1}(\Omega)^{\prime}. Then the bilinear form a(.,.)a(.,.) is defined by

a(U,V)=(T1(1+β)/2A1,T1(1+β)/2A2)L2+∫Ω(∇N1∇N2+ωN1N2)dx,\displaystyle a(U,V)=\left(T_{1}^{(1+\beta)/2}A_{1},T_{1}^{(1+\beta)/2}A_{2}\right)_{L^{2}}+\int_{\Omega}(\nabla N_{1}\nabla N_{2}+\omega N_{1}N_{2})dx,

where U=(A1,N1)U=(A_{1},N_{1}) and V=(A2,N2)V=(A_{2},N_{2}).

For any fixed α∈(0,Amin)\alpha\in(0,A_{\min}), we pick a function ϑα∈C∞​(ℝ)\vartheta_{\alpha}\in C^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}) such that ϑα​(s)=χ​log⁡s\vartheta_{\alpha}(s)=\chi\log s for s≥Amins\geq A_{\min}. Define Fα​(U)F_{\alpha}(U) by

Fα​(U)=(ψ​N​A​(1−A)+A~−∇(N∇ϑα(A))+ω),U=(A,N).\displaystyle F_{\alpha}(U)=\begin{pmatrix}\psi NA(1-A)+\tilde{A}\\ -\nabla(N\nabla\vartheta_{\alpha}(A))+\omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad U=(A,N).

and denote by (Pα)(P_{\alpha}) the modified problem (3).

As a consequence of Proposition 2.2, problem (Pα)(P_{\alpha}) admits a unique, maximal in time solution (A^,N^)(\hat{A},\hat{N}), defined in an interval [0,T∗)[0,T^{*}). Moreover, if T∗<∞T^{*}<\infty then limt→T∗‖A^​(t)‖H1+β+‖N^​(t)‖L2=∞\lim_{t\to T^{*}}\|\hat{A}(t)\|_{H^{1+\beta}}+\|\hat{N}(t)\|_{L^{2}}=\infty. Furthermore, it is classical for t>0t>0. This follows from a standard bootstrap argument based on parabolic regularity and imbedding theorems.

Observing that AminA_{\min} is a subsolution of the equation for A^\hat{A}, we deduce that A^≥Amin\hat{A}\geq A_{\min} in (0,T∗)(0,T^{*}), so that (A^,N^)(\hat{A},\hat{N}) actually solves the original problem (3).

As for local uniqueness for (3), the notion of solution to (3) implies that AA is uniformly positive on Ω¯×[0,T]\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T] for any 0<T<T∗0<T<T^{*} (since A∈C⁡([0,T∗),H1+β​(Ω))A\in C([0,T^{*});H^{1+\beta}(\Omega)). Since α\alpha can be arbitrary close to 00 in problem (Pα)(P_{\alpha}), the uniqueness for the original problem follows from the uniqueness for (Pα)(P_{\alpha}).

2.2. Basic estimates, energy identities and functional inequalities

Our first lemma provides the primary L1L^{1} control of NN and uniform lower and upper bounds for AA. The latter can be easily obtained from the maximum principle, owing to the special form of the nonlinear term in the equation for AA.

Lemma 2.1 (A priori estimates for AA and NN).

For all t∈(0,T∗)t\in(0,T^{*}), we have

A⁡(x,t)≥min⁡{1,A~,infA0​(x)}:=Amin,\displaystyle A(x,t)\geq\min\{1,\tilde{A},\inf A_{0}(x)\}:=A_{\min}, (18)
A⁡(x,t)≤max⁡{1,A~,supA0​(x)}:=Amax,\displaystyle A(x,t)\leq\max\{1,\tilde{A},\sup A_{0}(x)\}:=A_{\max}, (19)
N⁡(x,t)≥1−e−ω​t>0,\displaystyle N(x,t)\geq 1-e^{-\omega t}>0, (20)
‖N⁡(t)‖1=e−ω​t​‖N0‖1+|Ω|(1−e−ω​t),\displaystyle\|N(t)\|_{1}=e^{-\omega t}\|N_{0}\|_{1}+|\Omega|(1-e^{-\omega t}), (21)

hence in particular

‖N⁡(t)‖1≤max⁡{‖N0‖1,|Ω|}:=N1,max.\|N(t)\|_{1}\leq\max\{\|N_{0}\|_{1},|\Omega|\}:=N_{1,\max}. (22)
Proof.

To check (18) and (19), it suffices to observe that Amin,AmaxA_{\min},A_{\max} are, respectively, sub-/supersolution of the equation for AA, with Neumann boundary conditions, and to apply the maximum principle. The proof of (20) is similar, in view of the regularity of the solution. As for (21), it follows by integrating the equation for NN in space. ∎

We next state the basic energy identities.

Lemma 2.2 (Energy identities).

For all t∈(0,T∗)t\in(0,T^{*}), we have

12​dd​t​‖A⁡(t)‖22+‖A⁡(t)‖22+η​‖∇A​(t)‖22=ψ​∫ΩN​A2​(1−A)​𝑑x+∫ΩA~​A​𝑑x,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|A(t)\|_{2}^{2}+\|A(t)\|_{2}^{2}+\eta\|\nabla A(t)\|^{2}_{2}=\psi\int_{\Omega}NA^{2}(1-A)dx+\int_{\Omega}\tilde{A}A\,dx, (23)
12dd​t∥∇A(t)∥22+∥∇A(t)∥22+η∥ΔA(t)∥22=−ψ∫ΩNA(1−A)ΔAdx,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\nabla A(t)\|_{2}^{2}+\|\nabla A(t)\|_{2}^{2}+\eta\|\Delta A(t)\|^{2}_{2}=-\psi\int_{\Omega}NA(1-A)\Delta A\,dx, (24)
dd​t​∫Ω(N​log⁡N−N+1)​𝑑x+ω​∫Ω(N​log⁡N−N+1)​𝑑x+∫Ω|∇N|2N​𝑑x−∫Ω∇N.∇ϑ​(A)​𝑑x\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}(N\log N-N+1)dx+\omega\int_{\Omega}(N\log N-N+1)dx+\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla N|^{2}}{N}dx-\int_{\Omega}\nabla N.\nabla\vartheta(A)dx
=ω​∫Ω(log⁡N−N+1)​𝑑x≤0,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad=\omega\int_{\Omega}(\log N-N+1)dx\leq 0, (25)
12dd​t∥N(t)∥22+ω∥N(t)∥22+∥∇N(t)∥22=∫ΩN∇N.∇ϑ(A)dx+ω∫ΩNdx.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|N(t)\|_{2}^{2}+\omega\|N(t)\|_{2}^{2}+\|\nabla N(t)\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{\Omega}N\nabla N.\nabla\vartheta(A)dx+\omega\int_{\Omega}Ndx. (26)
Proof.

Formulae (23)-(26) follow by integration by parts after multipying, respectively, the first equation in (3) by AA and −Δ​A-\Delta A, and the second equation in (3) by log⁡N−1\log N-1 and NN. Note that these manipulations are licit in view of (20), of the classical regularity of NN and of the higher parabolic regularity applied to the equation for AA. ∎

Lemma 2.3 (Poincaré’s inequality).

For any uniformly positive function u∈H1​(Ω)u\in H^{1}(\Omega), there holds

‖u‖22≤μ2​‖u‖1​∫Ω|∇u|2u​𝑑x+|Ω|−1​‖u‖12,\displaystyle\|u\|_{2}^{2}\leq\mu^{2}\|u\|_{1}\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla u|^{2}}{u}dx+|\Omega|^{-1}\|u\|_{1}^{2}, (27)

where μ\mu is the best constant of the following Poincaré-Sobolev inequality:

≤μ2​‖∇u‖12+|Ω|​u¯2.\displaystyle\leq\mu^{2}\|\nabla u\|_{1}^{2}+|\Omega|\overline{u}^{2}. (29)

Since ‖∇u‖12≤‖u‖1​∫Ω|∇u|2u​𝑑x\|\nabla u\|_{1}^{2}\leq\|u\|_{1}\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla u|^{2}}{u}dx by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we deduce (27). ∎

A key ingredient in the proof of our main result is the following interpolation estimate. We recall that H2​(Ω)⊂C​(Ω¯)H^{2}(\Omega)\subset C(\overline{\Omega}), since we are in two space dimensions; however Lemma 2.4 remains true in any dimension if we assume u∈H2​(Ω)∩C⁡(Ω¯)u\in H^{2}(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega}).

Lemma 2.4.

Assume that u∈H2​(Ω)u\in H^{2}(\Omega) satisfies ∂u/∂ν=0\partial u/\partial\nu=0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega (in the sense of traces). Then

∫Ω|∇u|4​𝑑x≤K​osc2​(u)​∫Ω|Δ​u|2​𝑑x,\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{4}dx\leq K\,{\rm osc}^{2}(u)\int_{\Omega}|\Delta u|^{2}dx, (30)

where K=K⁡(Ω)>0K=K(\Omega)>0.

Proof.

Step 1. We first give a homogeneous version of the standard elliptic L2L^{2}-estimate, namely:

‖D2​u‖2:=(∑i​j‖uxi​xj‖22)1/2≤C⁡(Ω)​‖Δ​u‖2,\displaystyle\|D^{2}u\|_{2}:=\Bigl(\sum_{ij}\|u_{x_{i}x_{j}}\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2}\leq C(\Omega)\|\Delta u\|_{2}, (31)

To verify (31), we start from ‖D2​u‖2≤C⁡(Ω)​‖−Δ​u+u‖2\|D^{2}u\|_{2}\leq C(\Omega)\|-\Delta u+u\|_{2}, which is well known (see e.g. [7, Chapter 9]), hence

‖D2​u‖2≤C⁡(Ω)​(‖Δ​u‖2+‖u‖2).\displaystyle\|D^{2}u\|_{2}\leq C(\Omega)(\|\Delta u\|_{2}+\|u\|_{2}). (32)

Let (ek)k≥0(e_{k})_{k\geq 0} be a Hilbert basis of L2L^{2} made of eigenfunctions of −Δ-\Delta with domain H2H^{2} equipped with Neumann conditions. Denote the eigenvalues by λ0=0<λ1≤λ2≤…\lambda_{0}=0<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq... and observe that e0=C=C​o​n​s​t.e_{0}=C=Const. Set f=−Δ​uf=-\Delta u, decompose f=∑k≥0ck​ekf=\sum_{k\geq 0}c_{k}e_{k}, and note that

c0=(f,e0)=C∫Ωfdx=−C∫∂Ω∂νudσ=0.c_{0}=(f,e_{0})=C\int_{\Omega}f\,dx=-C\int_{\partial\Omega}\partial_{\nu}u\,d\sigma=0.

Let v:=∑k≥1λk−1​ck​ekv:=\sum_{k\geq 1}\lambda_{k}^{-1}c_{k}e_{k}. Then −Δ​v=f-\Delta v=f with ∂νv=0\partial_{\nu}v=0 and vv satisfies

‖v‖22=∑k≥1λk−2​|ck|2≤λ1−2​‖Δ​u‖22.\displaystyle\|v\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{k\geq 1}\lambda_{k}^{-2}|c_{k}|^{2}\leq\lambda_{1}^{-2}\|\Delta u\|_{2}^{2}. (33)

Since the difference z=v−uz=v-u satisfies Δ​z=0\Delta z=0, ∂νz=0\partial_{\nu}z=0, it follows that ∫Ω|∇z|2​𝑑x=0\int_{\Omega}|\nabla z|^{2}\,dx=0, so that

u=v+C​o​n​s​t.u=v+Const.

Combining this with (32) and (33), we obtain

‖D2​u‖2=‖D2​v‖2≤C⁡(Ω)​(‖Δ​v‖2+‖v‖2),\|D^{2}u\|_{2}=\|D^{2}v\|_{2}\leq C(\Omega)(\|\Delta v\|_{2}+\|v\|_{2}),

and

‖D2​u‖2≤C⁡(Ω)​(1+λ1−1)​‖Δ​u‖2.\|D^{2}u\|_{2}\leq C(\Omega)(1+\lambda_{1}^{-1})\|\Delta u\|_{2}.

Hence (31).

Step 2. By density, it suffices to prove the Lemma for u∈C2​(Ω¯)u\in C^{2}(\overline{\Omega}). We may assume without loss of generality that minΩ⁡u=0\min_{\Omega}u=0 and osc⁡(u)=‖u‖∞{\rm osc}(u)=\|u\|_{\infty}. For a matrix M=(mi​j)M=(m_{ij}), we denote |M|1=maxi⁡{∑j|mi​j|}|M|_{1}=\max_{i}\bigl\{\sum_{j}|m_{ij}|\bigr\}. Observing that

∇⋅(|∇u|2∇u)=|∇u|2Δu+2∇tu(D2u)∇u=∇tu(2D2u+(Δu)I)∇u,\nabla\cdot(|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u)=|\nabla u|^{2}\Delta u+2\,{}^{t}\nabla u(D^{2}u)\nabla u={}^{t}\nabla u\bigl(2D^{2}u+(\Delta u)I\bigr)\nabla u,

|∇⋅(|∇u|2∇u)|≤|2D2u+(Δu)I|1|∇u|2.\bigl|\nabla\cdot(|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u)\bigr|\leq\bigl|2D^{2}u+(\Delta u)I\bigr|_{1}|\nabla u|^{2}.

∫Ω|∇u|4​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{4}dx =∫Ω∇u⋅|∇u|2∇udx=−∫Ωu∇(|∇u|2∇u)dx\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\,dx=-\int_{\Omega}u\nabla(|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u)dx
≤∫Ωu​|2​D2​u+(Δ​u)​I|1​|∇u|2​𝑑x≤12​∫Ω|∇u|4​𝑑x+12​∫Ωu2|2​D2​u+(Δ​u)​I|12​𝑑x.\displaystyle\leq\int_{\Omega}u\bigl|2D^{2}u+(\Delta u)I\bigr|_{1}|\nabla u|^{2}dx\leq\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{4}dx+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}u^{2}\bigl|2D^{2}u+(\Delta u)I\bigr|_{1}^{2}dx.

Consequently,

∫Ω|∇u|4​𝑑x≤|u|∫Ω∞2|2​D2​u+(Δ​u)​I|12​𝑑x.\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{4}dx\leq\|u\|_{\infty}^{2}\int_{\Omega}\bigl|2D^{2}u+(\Delta u)I\bigr|_{1}^{2}dx. (34)

Since ∫Ω|2​D2​u+(Δ​u)​I|12​𝑑x≤C​‖D2​u‖22\int_{\Omega}\bigl|2D^{2}u+(\Delta u)I\bigr|_{1}^{2}dx\leq C\|D^{2}u\|_{2}^{2}, it follows from (31) that

We shall also need the following classical smoothing properties of the Neumann heat semigroup. For d,λ>0d,\lambda>0, we define the operator 𝒜=𝒜d,λ=−d​Δ+λ{\mathcal{A}}={\mathcal{A}}_{d,\lambda}=-d\Delta+\lambda on L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega), with domain D(𝒜)={v∈H2(Ω);∂A/∂ν=0 on ∂Ω (in the sense of traces)}D({\mathcal{A}})=\{v\in H^{2}(\Omega);\ \partial A/\partial\nu=0\hbox{ on $\partial\Omega$ (in the sense of traces)}\}. We denote by T​(t)=Td,λ​(t)T(t)=T_{d,\lambda}(t) the semigroup generated by 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}. It is well known that, for any 0≤m≤20\leq m\leq 2, 1≤p≤q≤∞1\leq p\leq q\leq\infty and any ϕ∈L2​(Ω)∩Lp​(Ω)\phi\in L^{2}(\Omega)\cap L^{p}(\Omega), we have

‖T⁡(t)​ϕ‖Wm,q​(Ω)≤C​e−λ​t​(1+t−m2−1p+1q)​‖ϕ‖Lp​(Ω),t≥0,\|T(t)\phi\|_{W^{m,q}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\lambda t}\bigl(1+t^{-\frac{m}{2}-\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}}\bigr)\|\phi\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)},\qquad t\geq 0, (36)

with C=C⁡(Ω,m,p,q,η)>0C=C(\Omega,m,p,q,\eta)>0.

6. Conclusion

In this article, we have considered a nonlinear, strongly coupled, parabolic system arising in the modeling of burglary in residential areas. The system involves two spatio-temporal unknowns: the attractivity value of the property and the criminal density. The system is of chemotaxis-type and involves a logarithmic sensivity function and specific interaction and relaxation terms. This model has appeared in [18], as a modification of the model of Short et al. [22]. In [18] some results about linearized stability/instability of the homogeneous steady-states and some numerical simulations suggesting the existence of hotspots were given. However, the (local and) global existence of solutions was left open.

In this article, under suitable assumptions on the data of the problem, we have given a rigorous proof of the existence of a global and bounded, classical solution, thereby solving the problem left open in [18]. In the range of anti-diffusion parameter χ\chi relevant for the criminological model, our sufficient condition for global existence roughly says that, at the initial time, the product of the oscillation of the attractivity value and of the total criminal population should not be two large. Our proofs are based on the construction of approximate entropies and on the use of various functional inequalities.

We have also provided explicit numerical conditions for global existence when the domain is a square, including concrete cases involving values of the parameters which are expected to be physically relevant. In such cases, in the range of diffusion parameter η\eta used by [22], our global existence conditions are compatible with magnitudes of attractivity which are up to about twice those of their static component. It is suggested in [18] that a ratio of order 10 (instead of 2) might be desirable, even for smaller values of η\eta that the ones we consider here. However, this is still beyond the range in which we can rigorously prove global existence (and actually, global existence for such systems need not be taken for granted, as shown by the existing chemotaxis literature).
